9d2ca314d060.content: On June 13, 2026, a shooting incident occurred in the Town of Ahoskie, North Carolina, in which multiple gunshots were fired into the residence of Sage and Sweetgrass at the Bradshaw House Inc.., a 501c3 nonprofit transitional housing program. According to reports, several adults and children were inside the home at the time. Bullets entered multiple areas of the residence, and a stray bullet struck and killed Dior, a 5-year-old American Bully who was inside her crate on the second floor of the home. The incident received coverage from regional media outlets, and the organization has been publicly seeking information from anyone who may know who was responsible. The shooting also reportedly caused damage to property associated with the nonprofit. From statements released by Sage & Sweetgrass, the organization has emphasized that: Multiple shots struck the occupied residence. Residents, including children, narrowly avoided injury. Dior was killed by a bullet that entered the home. The organization is calling for accountability and community assistance in identifying those responsible.

a29b21ae9c17.content: I am a person of reason and empathy, which is why I find it difficult to understand what happened after our transitional home— Sage and Sweetgrass at the Bradshaw House Inc. , the only program of its kind in Ahoskie—was riddled with bullets and our beloved 5-year-old American Bully, Dior, was killed by a stray bullet. The Ahoskie Police Department responded, and for that we are grateful. However, I believe that when a tragedy impacts a family, a nonprofit organization, or a business in our community, town leaders should rally around those affected and show support. It should not be the responsibility of the victim to make phone calls explaining what happened or asking for help. There should be follow-up visits, advocacy, and outreach. Community leaders should check on those impacted, offer resources, and help ensure their voices are heard. I also believe incidents of this magnitude deserve broader awareness. Media outlets should be notified, public officials should speak out against the violence, and social media should be used to keep the community informed and engaged. When gun violence strikes a home filled with families, children, and vulnerable individuals, and a life is lost—even the life of a beloved family pet—it should matter to the entire community. Communities grow stronger when they stand together, not just during celebrations, but also during moments of tragedy. We are still seeking accountability for the June 13, 2026 shooting at Sage & Sweetgrass at the Bradshaw House Inc. We remain committed to our mission of housing hope, not violence, and we hope our community will continue to stand with us as we seek justice for Dior and safety for all.

fc1af26d104e.content: What has been most difficult is not just the shooting itself, but the lack of visible community support afterward. Support matters. A phone call matters. A visit matters. A public statement matters. Asking, "How can we help?" matters. When a nonprofit organization serving families, children, seniors, veterans, and individuals experiencing housing instability is impacted by violence, the community should come together. Support from town officials, community leaders, businesses, churches, civic organizations, and residents can make a tremendous difference. Support is not about money. It is about showing up. It is about letting those affected know they are not alone. It is about advocating for justice, sharing information, checking in on victims, and standing united against violence. In times of tragedy, people should not have to ask their community to care. The community should care enough to show up on its own. That is the support we needed. That is the support we still need.

We drink soup from paper cups like it's coffee in the middle of the night, we use military time to set our alarm, we can finish a meal in 30 seconds standing up...behind a curtain & in between meal service & clearance. We hate when you stand up after the plane lands, we laugh when you clap after the plane lands. We love when you thank us. Aircraft is for Flight Attendants, Airplane is for passengers. We talk in dates even if it’s just the next day. We never know what day it is but we remember what supermarket is closest to our hotel. We are the best packers and can find anything we see in a magazine in the world, clothes, furniture,the best restaurants, best hotels, sightseeing excursions, etc... We may especially have loved working with someone specifically without knowing that person's name or if we will ever fly together again. “4L” or “1R” may be our names for the day. We all have woken up in the middle of the night with a mini heart attack forgetting where we are. We see beautiful places but no one to share the moment with. We walk through terminals as if time is endless—never knowing when it will be the final boarding, the last laugh on the jumpseat, the last story shared somewhere above the clouds. The smallest moments never feel like goodbyes… until they are. A plastic cup handed to a child. A quiet smile to a stranger. A routine flight that was never meant to be anything more than ordinary. We leave home believing we’ll return— never imagining that, somewhere across the world, a phone will ring… and a family’s life will be forever divided into before and after. A voice on the other end delivering the words no one is ever ready to hear: they’re not coming home this time. Tonight, my heart carries the weight of every life touched by the tragedy of Air Canada Flight 8646— the crew, the passengers, air traffic control, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey staff, and the families now left to hold what remains. There are no right words for a loss like this—only silence, grief, and remembrance. May your final journey be gentle. May the skies hold you softly. May you be carried home on endless tailwinds. We may wear different uniforms… but this pain, this love, this bond—we all share it. Forever #UnitedByWings”

640135aebc8a.content: A 3% raise doesn’t feel like much when the cost of living got a bigger bump than your paycheck. That’s why workers tune out when companies talk about “competitive annual raises.” If prices rise faster than your income, you’re not moving forward. You’re just losing ground a little more slowly. According to the BLS, real average hourly earnings fell 0.7% from May 2025 to May 2026. Paychecks got bigger in dollars, but buying power got smaller after inflation. So when employers hand out 2%, 3%, or 4% raises and expect applause, people notice. The grocery store noticed. The landlord noticed. The insurance company noticed. The utility bill noticed. Everyone got their increase except the person doing the work. And somehow employees are supposed to celebrate a raise that barely keeps up with falling behind. 7d5644ae65ad.content: There isn't a single state in America where someone working full-time at minimum wage can afford a basic two-bedroom apartment. Not one. The federal minimum wage is $7.25 an hour. The hourly wage needed to afford a modest two-bedroom apartment nationwide is $33.63. That's not a small gap. That's a canyon. At minimum wage, you'd need to work 116 hours a week to afford the rent. There are only 168 hours in a week. After that, you'd have 52 hours left for sleeping, eating, getting ready for work, spending time with family, and doing everything else life requires. And that's the national average. In California, the number is $49.61 an hour. In Massachusetts, it's $45.90. Even in West Virginia, the most affordable state on the list, it's $18.49. The federal minimum wage doesn't come close anywhere. And here's what gets missed. This stopped being only a minimum wage issue a long time ago. Nearly half of renters in America spend more than 30% of their income on housing. Of the 25 most common jobs in the country, 18 don't pay enough to meet the wage needed for a two-bedroom apartment. That's 74 million workers. People with jobs. People doing everything they're told they're supposed to do. Work hard. Show up. Be responsible. Yet the numbers still don't work. When housing costs rise faster than paychecks year after year, effort stops being the problem. The math becomes the problem. And that's what should make people pay attention.

5bd7493871dd.content: You can support funding schools, roads, firefighters, and local services while still recognizing that the property tax system has a serious flaw. But governments have many other sources of revenue besides taxing homeowners year after year. They collect income taxes, sales taxes, corporate taxes, tariffs, licensing fees, permit fees, tourism revenue, public land leases, investment income, and revenue from natural resources. In 2025 alone, the U.S. collected more than $210 billion in customs duties. The money exists. The options exist. Yet many seniors on fixed incomes are watching their property tax bills rise simply because the market says their home is worth more—not because their income increased. A home can double in value. A retiree's Social Security check usually doesn't. No one who spent decades paying off a mortgage should risk being taxed out of their home in retirement while governments continue to have numerous alternative sources of revenue available. Supporting schools and local services is important. Protecting seniors from losing their homes is important too. A fair system should be able to do both. #PropertyTaxes #CostOfLiving #HousingAffordability #TaxFairness #WorkingClass #MiddleClass

d0bbf53ce247.content: This is the question every working American should be asking—and the answer should concern everyone. The 2026 Social Security Trustees Report, released this week, now projects that the retirement trust fund will be depleted in 2032, a full year sooner than forecast last year. That's just six years away. Despite the headlines, Social Security isn't going away. Workers will keep paying payroll taxes, and benefits will continue to be issued. The problem is that once the trust fund runs out of reserves, the program can only pay out what it collects in real time—and that won't be enough to cover all promised benefits. If Congress does nothing, beneficiaries could face an automatic 22% cut in payments. That's a hard pill to swallow for millions of Americans who have spent decades contributing to the system with every paycheck. The promise was simple: pay in during your working years and receive benefits in retirement, supported by the next generation of workers. But the math has changed. Fewer workers are supporting a growing retiree population. Birth rates have fallen. Immigration has slowed. The system that once had a comfortable cushion is now under increasing strain. Over the next ten years, Social Security is expected to pay out roughly $3.8 trillion more than it brings in. Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have known this was coming for years, yet the problem remains largely unaddressed. If you're in your 40s or 50s, this isn't some distant policy debate—it's a retirement issue. Plan as if a 22% benefit cut is possible, and hope Washington finally acts before that becomes reality.

a478a22fb78a.content: I'd been refraining from making a post about this but the frustration has become too much. Freddie Highmore's "I am a Surgeon" breakdown scene in The Good Doctor is not a haha funny subject. It is a very real, albeit slightly dramatised, depiction of an autistic breakdown. Something that I deeply resonate with and relate to. The way he trembles as he sits down in the office chair, almost as if he's trembling from physically holding back his emotions. The raw shouting. The way his communication entirely breaks down until all he can do is scream "I am a surgeon!" in the most heartbreakingly frustrated tone of voice. The way he lashes out at his bag at the end of the scene. Would you laugh and make memes if you saw a recording of one of your autistic friends having a breakdown similar to his? Would you treat your autistic peers with the same callous manner you treat this character? I have suffered many, many breakdowns, meltdowns, and shutdowns in my life. There is still much to be done with regards to the depiction of autistic folk in tv and film, but depicting moments like this, in the way it has been shown, is a good start in terms of showing neurotypical audiences every side of being on the autistic spectrum. And what has society done in response to this representation? Laughed at it. Take your ableist memes and shove them.

c15bfb5b1640.content: Autism is in the news again and once again I'm having to hold my tongue on so many facebook posts where people completely and utterly succumb to survivorship bias. As we all know, autism is a spectrum disorder, so the presentations of it vary wildly. The presentations can range anywhere from things like: -Group 1: "Occasionally stims and talks more than socially appropriate about special interests." To things like: -Group 2: "Can't talk, smashes head into window when upset, and runs in front of traffic b/c they don't understand the dangers of getting hit by a car." Understand that these are *both* autism. One of these people can hold a job, live safely on their own, and can live a happy self-actualizing fulfilling life with some minor accommodations. Folks in this category really just need accommodations and occasionally some therapy. The other person needs lifelong live-in care-giving or to reside in some kind of facility devoted to institutional level care. Of these two groups* (*there are obviously many more presentations of autism, but I'm using these two to illustrate my point), one of them is online talking to other people about their autism, and one is not. What people online see then, is a non-stop parade of people with autism telling them how useful it is and how much they enjoy being unique. And so the public opinion of autism is shaped largely by those who are the least impacted by it. The people who are the most severely impacted by it, like those individuals in Group 2 that I mentioned, are not online, they are not sharing their stories, they are not communicating with the outside world beyond their care-givers. And they are forgotten and ignored by those in Group 1. That is the thing that angers me the most about this, the people who should understand the most are the ones ignoring the vulnerable population that cannot speak up for themselves. Worse still, when the care-givers of those individuals in Group 2 speak up, asking for solutions and cures for the very real life limiting disabilities of their loved ones, they get shouted down and bullied by Group 1. The group that doesn't actually need any of those interventions. Group 1 actively works to undermine Group 2 making any progress in their disability. It would be like if people who were "visually impaired" enough to occasionally need reading glasses, constantly tried to block research into solving the "visual impairment" of macular degeneration (which causes you to eventually go completely blind). That makes no logical sense and is utterly cruel. All of this would probably be solved if we actually differentiated the autistic folks who are only slightly inconvenienced verses the ones that are debilitatingly disabled. Autism-Aspergers and Autism-Primary or something. Whatever the science works out that makes the most sense. The point is, this is your regular "Autism is in the news again" reminder that the only autistic folks you actually hear from are those who are the least impacted by their autism. Please remember that there is a whole community of autistic folks who you don't hear from because they *can't* communicate like that, and just because Group 1 doesn't need something, doesn't mean that Group 2 doesn't need it. And Group 2 deserves to live happy self-actualizing fulfilling lives as much as Group 1 does.

0c91ce87c72e.content: Okay, kids, it's time for a story about our healthcare system. Back in 2008, I was put on a medication during an inpatient hospital stay. I have treatment-resistant anxiety as well as fibromyalgia, so the doctor immediately suggested pregabalin, which I hadn't been on before, because I'd exhausted just about everything else that isn't a benzodiazepine or opiate, which are not doctors' favorites for cases like mine. I responded extremely well, and I have been on it for almost the entire time since then, so close to a decade. Cue my recent insurance change because of our lovely system where your insurance is tied to your employer. Casey's last contract ended and I unexpectedly lost my job within a couple weeks of each other at the end of 2018. We both got new jobs, and I'm not yet eligible for coverage at mine, so that meant we had to take his, switching from Aetna to Anthem BCBS. Anthem requires pre-authorization for pregabalin, so I had a very short window to make that happen before my last prescription fill ran out. Because they didnt send us new cards for weeks and about everything else went wrong, I wasn't getting a decision and had to start paying $112 a week for medication I'm dependent on to function normally. I found out a couple days ago that they were refusing to cover it because gabapentin is a cheaper alternative. Now, I'm a biochemist by schooling, so I know they're very similar - enough that I've complained that pregabalin is a scheduled drug while gabapentin isn't, something I've done plenty because of the headaches it causes me. But I'm also a patient, and there's a reason the doctor put me on pregabalin, not gabapentin. That doctor regularly prescribes gabapentin; he thought pregabalin made more sense for me. So my current prescriber, who has had me on pregabalin for years, tried to fight for me, but they refused. It's shitty enough on its own to deny a drug someone needs and they've been on for a decade, but it gets worse. Now, note before I continue: use of pregabalin for psychiatric purposes is off-label, even though it's been done for years, and many insurance plans cover it, like my old one. It was initially prescribed by a psych provider, so my current psych provider is the one that's been writing my script. Because I'm using pregabalin for both psychiatric and neurologic care, I can go to my primary care doctor and have her write me the exact same prescription that my other prescriber has been writing me for years. I'll need to go through pre-auth again, and they'll probably give my doctor a hard time, but they'll ultimately more likely than not approve it. But since the "wrong" doctor is writing it, they say no even after years showing that this drug helps prevent expensive inpatient hospital stays for me. This literally makes no financial sense for them, and it means I have to wait weeks for an appointment to get back on my original medication. (I've been temporarily put on gabapentin so I can do things like go to work and, you know, feed myself, stuff like that. Hopefully I don't experience any major side effects. I'm in more pain today than usual. Fingers crossed that's chance.) But, okay, fine, we can chalk that up to playing by the rules. Fair enough. But it gets worse yet again. I went to the pharmacy today to pick up another prescription, this one a cheap one that I've been on for even longer. The pharmacist told me they hadn't been able to fill it because my insurance said I was trying to fill it too soon. I said that was impossible because I was on new insurance, my old plan was expired, and I hadn't filled this script since then. I should've been able to fill it again the day I switched to a new plan. So what gives? It turns out, even though I have a new insurance plan through a completely different provider, my prescriptions are being processed through the same system (many providers use the same system to handle prescriptions separate from other medical care). So the prescription provider won't give me a drug I've been on for a decade because of the magical line in the sand when I switched to a new plan, but they also won't give me a script I've been on for even longer even though I'm on a new plan. I'm being denied both of my medications for the exact opposite reasons. Medications I need to function. Medications that prevent me from $30k hospital stays. Weird flex, but okay.

SO much more true than it just being a cute lil proverb. Human beings were not made to live in isolation. We are a group animal. Our species survival depends on making use of everyone's talents. Allowing each person to specialize where they are especially innovative. Allowing many to work as a team to get big jobs done. If you look at your friends and neighbors and relatives, you could make a list of your commonalities with them. It would be long. But then you could identify the unique parts of each person's personality as well. Likely even their strengths, that differ from each others. Like Yin and Yang, humans survive best when we balance our uniqueness and our commonalities. We work best when we work as a team to ensure the survive of all of us - and - when we respect each person's unique strengths. How many of us, be real, could survive for 5 years on this earth in the wilderness, with no goods or food made by other people, all by ourselves. Like, you walk into the woods with nothing you didn't create with your hands and that's it. No tools. No clothes. Just you and your hands and feet. That's all you get. Including 5 nice snowy cold winters over your 5 year trial. Some of you could. Most could not. And fewer than you think. Because in your head, you are just thinking of the obvious right? Food, shelter, clothing created with your hands in the wilderness? But it takes more than wilderness survival skills to make it. Because as it turns out, great wilderness skills aren't the only skill that is needed. Survival depends on working as a team so that when our special strength is needed, it is there and has been nurtured. But survival also depends on our taking care of each other. Working as a team that is cohesive and caring. If you are human, it really does take a village.

66a7ad9f6c72.content: I lied to a customer this morning. Said it straight to her face. And honestly? I’d do it again tomorrow. I’ve been a mechanic for 30 years. My hands are permanently stained with grease, my back is a roadmap of old injuries, and I run my shop with a simple rule: Fix it right. Charge what it’s worth. No exceptions. At 8 a.m., a beat-up Chevy limped into my lot coughing smoke like it needed last rites. A young woman stepped out — couldn’t have been more than 22 — wearing oversized nursing scrubs and exhaustion in her eyes. In the back seat, a baby slept in a car seat, clutching a tiny teddy bear with one ear missing. “It’s making a weird noise,” she said quietly. “Please… please tell me it’s something small.” I popped the hood. It wasn’t small. It wasn’t even medium. It was a disaster — burst hose, shredded belt, leaking oil, one bad drive away from blowing the engine. “To fix this right,” I told her gently, “you’re looking at about a thousand dollars.” She didn’t cry. She didn’t panic. She just stared at her baby. Then at her phone. Then at the ground. “I start my new job at the nursing home in an hour,” she whispered. “If I’m late… they’ll fire me. I don’t have anything left in my account. I was going to put water in it and just… try.” She gently placed a hand on the hood like she was apologising to the car for being poor. That did it. I swear, sometimes life gives you a moment where doing the right thing isn’t a choice — it’s a responsibility. “Give me your keys,” I said. “I can’t pay you,” she said immediately, panic rising again. “Did I ask you for money?” I replied. She blinked at me, unsure. “The part you need,” I lied smoothly, “is on national backorder. Two weeks minimum. You can’t drive this car.” She looked like she was going to collapse. “Two weeks? How do I—how am I supposed to get to work?” I pulled my truck keys out of my pocket and held them out. “Take mine.” Her jaw dropped. “Sir… that’s your truck.” “I know. Built like a tank. It’ll get you to work and back. Bring it back when your car’s done.” She stared at me like she couldn’t decide whether to cry or hug me. My shop manager looked at me like I’d lost my mind. But I’ve been young and broke. I’ve been terrified of losing a job. I’ve been one bill away from falling apart. So she left safely, in my truck, with her baby strapped in the back. And her old Chevy stayed in my garage. There was no backorder. The hose cost $20. But I didn’t stop there. Every lunch break. Every after-hours minute. Every quiet moment in the shop… I rebuilt that car. Brand new tires. Fixed the belt. Cleaned the engine. Rewired the lights. Replaced the brake pads. Oil change. Detailed the interior. Tuned the engine until it purred like it hadn’t purred in years. By the time I was done, that 15-year-old junker felt like a brand-new ride. Two weeks later, she walked back into the shop, my truck keys in hand. “It drove perfectly,” she said softly. “Thank you. Truly. I’m… nervous to see the bill.” I handed her the invoice. TOTAL: $0.00 PAID IN FULL BY FACTORY WARRANTY RECALL. Another lie. A harmless one. A necessary one. She stared at the paper. Then at the car. Then at me. “But… this isn’t a new car,” she whispered. “There can’t be a recall.” “Ma’am,” I said, pretending to fuss with paperwork, “you questioning my paperwork accuracy?” She laughed through tears — that soft, heartbreaking laugh people make when the world finally gives them a break instead of another burden. “Why would you do all this?” she whispered. I looked at her sleeping baby in her arms. “Because you’re trying,” I said. “And the world doesn’t make it easy for people who are trying.” She hugged me. Tight. One of those hugs you feel in your bones. When she drove away in that bright, reliable Chevy, waving out the window, I stood there a long time… thinking. About how many times I wished someone would help me when I was young. About how much difference a little kindness makes. About how good it feels to make someone feel safe — even for a moment. People often say, “You can’t help everyone.” Maybe not. But you can help someone. And sometimes that someone is exactly who needed it that day. So yes — I lied this morning. I lied to give a young mom a chance. I lied to make sure a baby got to daycare safely. I lied so someone wouldn’t lose the job they desperately needed. And if I had to do it again? I’d lie every single time. Because the kindness we give away… is the only part of us that lasts. 💛 Moral: Be the break in someone’s bad day. Be the yes in their world full of no. Be the reason they still believe good people exist. #spiritualgrowth
